body.text: Coalition unveils plans to partly privatise Melbourne's sewerage and axe level crossing removals
In short:
The Coalition has released its costed plans for spending and saving, two days out from the November 28 state election.
If elected, the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) expects the Coalition's policies to lower net debt by $20 billion over four years.
What's next?
Opposition leader Jess Wilson says it's a matter for Victorians how they vote with the information they have at the time.
Opposition Leader Jess Wilson will partly privatise Melbourne's sewerage network, cut and delay level crossing removals and walk back Labor plans to expand free kindergarten if elected on Saturday.
Ms Wilson, who is also the shadow treasurer, defended releasing the policies more than a week after early voting opened. More than 1.6 million Victorians have already voted.
"That's a matter for Victorians," Ms Wilson said, two days before the election.
"Victorians decide when they vote and decide why they vote and with the information that they have at that time.
"We're releasing them in full for Victorians today."
Recycled sewage treatment privatisation policy promises savings

The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) tallied up the cost of Ms Wilson's policies, finding that net debt would be $20 billion lower over four years under the Coalition, down to $176 billion. This would also reduce the Victorian interest bill.

The main benefit to the budget is leasing Melbourne Water's Eastern and Western sewage treatment plants under the "asset recycling program". This would add $13.63 billion to state coffers by 2030-31, including land sales.
The Coalition has taken this policy to its last two elections.

Ms Wilson in August said she "wouldn't touch" Melbourne Water when pressed on whether it could be privatised, and on Thursday rejected that a long-term lease amounted to privatisation. Labor has previously looked at privatising the assets.
Ms Wilson insisted that household water bills would not go up under the model, despite a poor track record of privatising the sewerage network overseas.
Environmental group Clean Ocean Foundation expressed alarm over the proposal, arguing the part-privatisation presented a "clear and present danger to Victoria's coastlines, rivers and waterways".
"Wastewater treatment is not simply an infrastructure investment opportunity; it is a critical environmental safeguard," the group said.

"Private operators have commercial incentives that may conflict with the public interest, particularly when it comes to costly treatment upgrades, emerging contaminants, nutrient removal and pollution prevention.
"We cannot afford to compromise environmental standards or allow the pursuit of private returns to come at the expense of the health of our marine and freshwater environments."
Change of plans for free kinder, level crossing upgrade plans
Ms Wilson also revealed that a Coalition government would not expand free kindergarten to 30 hours a week for four-year-olds, up from 15 hours, as is existing Labor government policy.
"We will also guarantee free kinder in a responsible and disciplined fashion by making the scheme sustainable," she said.
"By keeping the rollout at 15 hours per week, we can guarantee free kinder in the future."
The Coalition was looking to allow providers to charge a gap fee under the "free kinder" model, but Ms Wilson ruled that out on Thursday.
If elected, Ms Wilson said her government would also cancel the level crossing removals in Yarraville, Spotswood, and all those along the Upfield line in Brunswick and Parkville.
Level crossing removals in Seaford would be delayed beyond 2030.
Yarraville and Spotswood are already contracted, which Ms Wilson said would cost $90 million to break, ultimately saving $2.127 billion. Of that, $1.2 billion is within the forward estimates.
She also weakened her commitment to reach a cash surplus by 2032, clarifying that this was the 2033 financial year.
Economists have previously doubted the Coalition's ability to reach the commitment, a critique seized upon by Labor.
Road maintenance investment boost, as public service spend drops
Ms Wilson has relied on her plan to reduce the Victorian Public Service (VPS) through attrition — estimated to save $5.69 billion by 2030-31 — would help reach that goal.
Nationals leader Danny O'Brien said the Transport Accident Commission (TAC) scheme was over-funded, which would be re-invested in road maintenance.
The PBO expects this measure to save about $3.4 billion over the forward estimates.
But independent economist Saul Eslake cautioned that it could result in "compulsory third-party insurance premiums going up by more than they might otherwise".
"That hasn't been spelled out in the document," he said.
Ms Wilson had been under pressure to explain how she would reduce debt while promising to spend more than Labor and cutting taxes.
The PBO costings said expenditure under the Coalition would reduce by $3.246 billion over four years, while revenue would reduce by $590.9 million.
The Coalition would draw down $5.734 billion from unallocated contingency funding, set aside for unexpected costs, to pay off debt.
"There is emergency contingency funds that remain," Ms Wilson said. "This is unallocated contingencies."
The Coalition has counted on selling renewable energy projects owned by the State Electricity Commission (SEC) to gain $1 billion, including battery projects and the Delburn Wind Farm.

Ms Wilson insisted that pausing and reviewing the $35 billion SRL East rail line between Cheltenham and Box Hill will not have an impact on the budget, given she said she would continue work on all existing contracts.
"We don't know the contracts for the SRL," she said.
The Coalition would also sell the air rights to the Richmond station precinct.
Measures lack 'tough decisions'
The question of how the opposition would fund promises to both cut taxes and create new spending measures has loomed over the election campaign.
RMIT public policy professor David Hayward said today's announcements identified where the money would come from, but a lack of "tough decisions" could create fiscal headaches in the future.
"Economist will say more needs to be done to get the budget under control, and selling assets to pay down debt is a temporary fix rather than a long-term one," he said.
Labor was highly critical of the Coalition's plans while releasing its own costings, particularly Ms Wilson's plans for the sewerage system.
"To dump this out two days before the election shows a level of cynicism that means she does not deserve to be premier," Treasurer Colin Brooks said.
"You cannot mislead people this way and expect to be elected premier."
Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the Liberals' plan to partly privatise the sewerage system "frankly stinks".
"It will be a disaster and lead to skyrocketing bills just like it did in the UK," Ms Sandell said.
